newsitem.title: UK: Blair and Clinton set to hit it off.
newsitem.headline: Blair and Clinton set to hit it off.

text.p: Tony Blair crowns a giddy first month as Britain's prime minister on Thursday by welcoming to Downing Street one of the men who inspired his landslide election victory -- U.S. President Bill Clinton.

While the visit will allow the two leaders to swap notes on a range of issues, British officials said it would be primarily an opportunity to cement ties that go deeper than the political links between Blair's Labour party and Clinton's Democrats.

"He (Blair) and Clinton get on extremely well. They have got a very good personal relationship. They have a very keen mutual interest in certain issues such as education and welfare reform," one Blair aide said.
Indeed, the stopover, on Clinton's way home from a NATO-Russian summit in Paris and a Marshall Plan commemoration in the Hague, could slip into a mutual-admiration session.
Clinton was the first foreign leader to congratulate Blair on his victory in the early hours of May 2 and described him as an exciting and able man. "I like him very much," he said.
Blair is honouring Clinton by inviting him to say a few words to his assembled cabinet ministers at the end of their weekly meeting -- a rare mark of respect, if not unprecedented.
President Richard Nixon spoke to then Labour prime minister Harold Wilson's cabinet in 1969.

Still, for a fledgling administration that is keenly aware of the importance of political symbols, the invitation is a powerful way for Blair to herald a revival of the so-called special relationship between Washington and London.
Although Clinton praised defeated prime minister John Major, with whom he worked for five years, disputes over Bosnia and Northern Ireland made their relations rocky at times.
Moreover, no one ever forgot that Major's Conservative party openly helped Clinton's Republican opponent, former president George Bush, in the 1992 race for the White House.
Now the stars are properly aligned.

Labour makes no secret of the lessons it learned from Clinton's campaigning -- particularly the need to rebut political attacks instantly and to focus laser-like on the crucial middle ground where elections are won and lost.
Links between the Democrats and Labour are close.
Clinton's former pollster, Stan Greenberg, came to London to help out with a campaign that political analysts deemed presidential in style.
The superficial similarities between Blair and Clinton tend to reinforce the political affinities.

Both are young and boyish. Both are natural campaigning politicians. Both attended Oxford University and their wives -- who will lunch together on Thursday -- have brought up children while maintaining careers as high-flying lawyers.

But as several British commentators have noted, there is also a big difference. Blair, with a parliamentary majority of 179, can in effect ram through whatever laws he likes, while Clinton constantly has to battle the Republican-led Congress.
So Clinton the master could be forgiven for shaking his head with envy when he calls on Blair, the fast-learning pupil.

"Mr Clinton may lead the most powerful nation on earth, but Mr Blair, for now, leads a government with far more power at home than Mr Clinton, or any American president, will ever enjoy," The Economist wrote recently.
